title: Word Chaining: An Efficient and Effective Alternative to Oral Phonemic Awareness
author: Anjanette McNeely
summary: McNeely, a classroom teacher, argues that oral-only phonemic awareness instruction from a popular program lacks strong evidence and that teachers should shift time to word chaining. She cites a 2022 meta-analysis finding that phonemic awareness paired with letters produces roughly twice the outcomes, and comments from Shanahan, Ehri and Burns that it should be taught with letters. She acknowledges the frustration of being told to abandon recently adopted practices, but frames following the science as accepting bumps and detours. She describes word chaining as practising encoding and decoding while making blending and segmenting concrete, and reports kindergarten gains in blending CVC and nonsense words after switching. Her closing metaphor is that following the science is slower and less glamorous than silver bullets.
points: Phonemic awareness taught with letters appears to produce about twice the outcomes of oral-only instruction, so isolated sound work is a weaker use of time.
Teacher frustration at repeated reversals is real, but science is self-correcting and practice should change when evidence shows something better.
Word chaining lets students practise encoding and decoding together, making blending and segmenting concrete.
Her own classroom evidence was gains on PA scores but not blending with the oral program, then real growth in blending after switching to word chains.
quotes: A 2022 meta-analysis by Rehfeld and colleagues found that phonemic awareness instruction paired with letters produced twice the outcomes of instruction without letters. Dr. Timothy Shanahan and Dr. Linnea Ehri have publicly stated that phonemic awareness should be taught with letters, not in isolation.

So what is a teacher supposed to do? Burns points out that if we truly followed the science, this program — along with many other education fads — would never have made it into classrooms. But they have.

The frustration teachers feel when asked to abandon practices they were just encouraged to adopt is real and understandable. As a classroom teacher, I know the exhaustion of constantly being told to change without clear explanations or meaningful training.

Yet, as I continue this journey to understand and apply the science, I’ve learned to accept the bumps and detours — and to change my practice when the evidence shows something works better. Professor Pamela Snow has recently reminded us, “Science is ultimately self-correcting over time, so these debates are important and mean we need to refresh our conceptual frameworks and everyday practice.

When I used Heggerty in my classroom, I noticed some gains in phonemic awareness scores, but I didn’t see improvement in students’ ability to blend words — which is the real goal of reading. That classroom experience mirrors what research is showing. After shifting to word chains, I saw significant growth in my kindergarteners’ ability to blend CVC words, especially nonsense words.
